Chapter Five: Ideas Are Energetic Visitors—It’s Up to Us to Respond.
Have you ever noticed how creative ideas seem to pop up out of nowhere? One minute, you’re just living your life, and the next—bam!—an idea lands in your mind, almost like it’s knocking at your door, asking to be let in.
These flashes of inspiration can feel both exciting and a little mysterious. Sometimes, they show up when you least expect them—maybe while you’re walking the dog, or just about to fall asleep. And even though they often arrive at the most inconvenient moments, they’re really invitations, little nudges from the universe, asking if you’ll listen.
Imagine this: someone is out for a walk, lost in thought, when suddenly an image for a story appears in their mind. It’s vivid, almost impossible to ignore. But life is busy—there’s laundry waiting, emails piling up, errands that can’t be put off. Still, the idea lingers, gently tugging, refusing to let go. Eventually, curiosity wins out—they sit down to write, unsure of where the story will lead. Just by saying “yes” and giving the idea some attention, something special begins to unfold.
Here’s something to remember: ideas aren’t things we own. They’re more like visitors—energetic guests that drift in and out, hoping to find someone willing to bring them to life. If we ignore them, they might wander off and find someone else who’s ready. It’s a humbling thought, but also a freeing one. Instead of feeling pressured to claim every idea as our own, we get to play, explore, and see where each creative visitor might lead us.
There’s a wonderful story about a writer who worked on a novel for years, only to lose passion for it halfway through. The spark faded, the idea slipped away. Later on, they discovered that someone else, living halfway across the world, had written an almost identical story. It’s as if the idea, wanting to be born, simply moved on to a new collaborator. Missing out on an idea isn’t a failure—it’s just part of the creative dance. Ideas have lives of their own and will keep searching until they find someone ready to help them grow.
So, what does it take to respond to an idea? Not expertise. Not certainty. Just a little attention and the willingness to give it a try. The process can be messy, unpredictable—even a bit scary—but it’s also incredibly rewarding. When you bring an idea to life, you’re not working alone. You’re partnering with something bigger than yourself, co-creating with the very spark that inspired you.
It’s so easy to talk ourselves out of acting on ideas. Maybe you think you’re not ready, or you don’t have enough talent. But remember, ideas don’t need perfection—they just need you to show up. Even a small effort, a little time spent experimenting or exploring, is usually enough to keep the creative flow alive.
Over time, you start to realize that ideas are gifts, not burdens. They’re opportunities to see the world differently, to find new parts of yourself, and to connect with others in ways you never expected. The invitation is always there: do you want to say “yes” and see where it leads, or let it pass by? Either way, the dance keeps going—and there will always be new ideas waiting for you to notice.
